The material used in the study was a nickel-based single-crystal superalloy G-Ni 135SX (MD2).
The single-crystal rods were prepared in the [111] orientation and used to manufacture cylindrical dog-bone specimens for low-cycle fatigue (LCF) experiments.
The LCF tests were performed at room temperature (24°C) and 825°C, with strain amplitudes of 0.6%, 0.8%, and 1.0%.
The in-situ SEM fatigue crack growth experiments were carried out at room temperature (24°C) and 650°C, with a peak stress of 680 MPa and a load ratio of 0.1.
The CP model considered only 12 equivalent {111} <110> slip systems, as there was no evidence of the activation of cubic slip systems in FCC crystals.
The elastic moduli for the cubic crystal (C11, C12, C44) were determined from the monotonic part of the cyclic loading curves.
The exponent n and the reference shear strain rate γ0 were chosen to consider the rate-dependent sensitivity and numerical stability.
The other CP model parameters related to the octahedral slip systems were determined by matching the [111] loading experiment data.
The critical ICSS value was linearly interpolated from 0.026 at 24°C to 0.020 at 650°C based on the critical resolved shear stress and stage I stress.
The energy-based exponential function used to describe the damage evolution of XFEM elements had an exponent of 2 and a dissipated energy of 0.001.
The maximum time increment was set to 0.01 seconds to avoid numerical instability and reduce the influence of partially damaged elements.
The 2D plane strain model covered an area of 2000×5000 μm2 near the notch root of the specimen, with a dense mesh of quadrilateral linear plane strain XFEM elements.
A predefined crack was introduced at the center of the notch in the XFEM area to reflect the initiation of the crack observed experimentally.
The manual control procedure was introduced to handle situations where the XFEM method could not properly capture sharp crack deflections or conflicting crack growth directions.
The mesh sensitivity study showed that the crack growth predictions from the two mesh sizes were similar, as long as the manual control of the crack path was kept consistent.
